Half of this is true, which is why it's so persistent. The famous deadlock comes from UI apps and classic ASP.NET, where an

must resume on the very thread that's blocked waiting for it. That can't happen in ASP.NET Core. The code returns the right value, and at low traffic it's as fast as the async version. One thread waiting 200 ms sounds like a rounding error.
The cost isn't one thread, though. It's one thread per request in flight, taken from a shared pool that grows slowly on purpose.
A blocked thread is a lost thread
ASP.NET Core runs every request on the
, the thread goes back to the pool while the HTTP call is in flight and serves other requests. With

, it stays parked until the call returns, doing nothing. Fifty concurrent requests to a 200 ms call need about fifty threads instead of a handful. The best practices page is direct about the result: many blocking calls "lead to Thread Pool starvation and degraded response times".
The pool adds threads slowly, by design

The pool creates threads on demand up to a minimum, which by default equals the processor count. Past that point it creates threads gradually, because too many threads compete for the CPU. Since .NET 6 it reacts faster when threads block on a task: some extra threads come without delay, then each new one waits a little longer, and when physical memory is short, injection slows down further. Until enough threads exist, new requests wait in the queue, including ones that would finish instantly.
The work that releases them waits in the same queue
The blocked thread is waiting for a task to complete, and completing it means running the code after the

. That code needs a pool thread as well, and it's queued behind incoming requests. Every new thread the pool adds may pick up a new request and block too. It's a deadlock in slow motion that only ends when the pool has added enough threads. That's

content.text: A higher minimum makes the first minutes look better, so it's tempting as a hotfix. The docs warn that raising it unnecessarily can cause performance problems, and every extra thread costs memory. The blocked threads are still there; you've only paid for them in advance. Use it, if at all, as a stopgap while the call chain becomes async.
